title: The violent patient: de-escalation and restraint
stem: Resus side room. A 60-year-old man was found lying on the street and brought in. He is now shouting, throwing a chair, and threatening staff. He smells of alcohol and has a graze on his forehead. Security and two nurses are nearby. Manage him.
notes:
Checked against NICE NG10 (Violence and aggression: short-term management, 2015), the HA restraint policy, and ACEP (2023) on agitation.

Step up in order: de-escalation (calm, space, one person talking, exits, listen, choices, reality orientation), then oral medication offered, then rapid tranquillisation (IM lorazepam; or IM haloperidol with promethazine; or IM olanzapine — NICE; HK EDs also use IM midazolam), with physical restraint only as needed to give it, the least restrictive, proportionate, for the shortest time, never prone for long, with a doctor present, and regular observations (every 15 minutes: pulse, BP, SpO2, respiratory rate, consciousness, circulation of limbs). ECG before haloperidol when possible (QT).

Think of the medical causes: hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury (a graze in a drunk man is a head injury until proved otherwise), sepsis, drug withdrawal, intoxication. Once sedated: glucose, examine, CT head as indicated.

'Excited delirium syndrome' in your notes is no longer an accepted diagnosis (ACEP withdrew support in 2023); describe it as hyperactive delirium with severe agitation and treat the cause. The 'geographic tongue sign' in your notes has no basis. Your de-escalation list matches.

steps.label: Talk to him
steps.hint: Safe distance, calm voice, introduce, listen, offer choices, set limits.

turns.line: GET AWAY FROM ME! Where am I? You've kidnapped me!

opts.t: [From a safe distance, door behind me, calm voice] Sir, I'm Dr Chan. You're in the hospital. You're safe. What's your name?
opts.mark: Keeps a safe distance, introduces self, orientates calmly

opts.t: You were found lying on the street and you've hurt your head. I'd like to help. Would you sit down and let us check your sugar with a small finger prick?
opts.mark: Offers a clear choice and a reason

steps.label: Medical causes
steps.hint: Glucose, oxygen, head injury, infection, drugs.

steps.label: Drug cart
steps.hint: Treat hypoglycaemia; if still dangerous, rapid tranquillisation.

opts.t: IV 10% glucose (or oral if he'll drink), then thiamine
opts.mark: Treats hypoglycaemia (with thiamine in alcohol use)

opts.t: If still dangerous: IM lorazepam 1–2 mg (or midazolam) with minimum restraint
opts.mark: Rapid tranquillisation if needed, with minimal restraint

opts.r: NICE: combine with promethazine to reduce dystonia, and check the ECG first.

steps.label: After he settles
steps.hint: Observations every 15 min, head injury assessment, document, debrief.

opts.t: Observations every 15 minutes: pulse, BP, SpO2, RR, GCS, limb circulation
Full examination and CT head: head injury in an intoxicated man
Document the incident, restraint time and reasons; staff debrief
Keep him prone and restrained until morning
opts.r: Prolonged prone restraint risks positional asphyxia; release as soon as safe.

qs.a: De-escalation, oral medication, rapid tranquillisation, restraint only as needed

qs.q: Why give thiamine to a malnourished alcohol user?

qs.a: At least every 15 minutes for the first hour

badge.name: De-escalator
badge.flavor: Distance, voice, choices. Sugar before sedation.

cards.q: First step with a violent patient?
Medical cause of aggression to check immediately?

options: IM lorazepam or IM haloperidol + promethazine
